Renal and Genitourinary Disorders

Urologic Stone Disease

Renal colic is common, painful, and usually dischargeable, but the misses are dangerous: AAA/vascular mimics, infected obstruction, solitary kidney obstruction, pregnancy, and renal failure risk.

Board trap: Stone plus fever, pyuria with systemic illness, renal insufficiency, solitary/transplanted kidney, or uncontrolled symptoms is not routine renal colic.

Urologic Stone Disease

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

Urologic stone disease has rising prevalence and recurrence. ED management focuses on diagnosis, analgesia, infection recognition, renal function risk, likelihood of passage, and need for urology.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Stones form when urine becomes supersaturated and inhibitors such as citrate/magnesium are insufficient. Calcium stones dominate; struvite stones are infection-related, uric acid stones form in acidic urine, cystine stones reflect cystinuria, and some medications create radiolucent stones.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen adds visual localization of ureter narrowing and CT hydronephrosis examples; Tintinalli remains the Ch94 spine and supplies every Ch94 table/figure.

Pain comes from ureteral obstruction, spasm, and hydronephrosis. Passage depends on stone size, shape, location, and obstruction degree; distal and smaller stones pass more often.

CLINICAL FEATURES

Classic renal colic is abrupt severe flank pain radiating to lower abdomen/groin with nausea/vomiting and restlessness. Distal stones may cause urgency, frequency, dysuria, and testicular/labial radiation. Stones do not explain hypotension; in older first-time patients, think AAA or vascular catastrophe.

Table 94-2

Risk factors for poor outcome with stones.

Risk factors for poor outcomes include renal function at risk, history of difficult stones, and infection. These patients need lower threshold for imaging, labs, urology, or admission.

DIAGNOSIS

Diagnosis is suspected clinically and supported by hematuria, but imaging confirms stone location and complications. Differential diagnoses include ureteral, renal, GU, GI, gynecologic, and vascular emergencies.

Tintinalli source

Table 94-3

Differential diagnoses for ureterolithiasis.

LABORATORY EVALUATION

UA supports hematuria and infection assessment, but hematuria may be absent. Culture sterile pyuria or infection concern. Check creatinine when renal risk exists and pregnancy test when applicable. Leukocytosis alone does not prove infection.

IMAGING

Image first-time stones, unclear diagnosis, high-risk hosts, suspected complications, and when follow-up is uncertain. Recurrent young stable patients with classic symptoms may not need immediate CT if risks are low.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen adds visual localization of ureter narrowing and CT hydronephrosis examples; Tintinalli remains the Ch94 spine and supplies every Ch94 table/figure.

Noncontrast CT is most sensitive and identifies alternative diagnoses. KUB can follow a known radiopaque stone after CT localization. Ultrasound is first line in pregnancy and useful for hydronephrosis, but can miss small/mid-ureter stones.

TREATMENT

ED treatment includes analgesia, antiemetics, judicious fluids, infection evaluation, and selected medical expulsive therapy. Forced IV hydration does not improve pain or passage and should not replace symptom-guided fluids.

PAIN AND NAUSEA

NSAIDs are first line when safe; opioids are added for refractory pain. Antiemetics and oral tolerance determine discharge readiness.

URINARY TRACT INFECTION

An obstructing stone with infection is a urologic emergency. Give antibiotics and obtain urgent drainage by stent or nephrostomy; antibiotics alone may fail without source control.

MEDICAL EXPULSION THERAPY

Tamsulosin may reduce time to passage for selected distal stones, especially larger stones over 5 mm. It is not a substitute for drainage when infection, renal risk, or uncontrolled symptoms exist.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

Discharge low-risk patients with controlled pain/nausea, no infection, no renal insufficiency, likely passage, reliable follow-up, analgesics/antiemetics, strainer, and return precautions. Discuss large, irregular, proximal, infected, solitary kidney, transplanted kidney, renal insufficiency, or uncontrolled cases with urology.

Tintinalli source

Table 94-5

Indications for admission in nephrolithiasis.

SPECIAL POPULATIONS/CONSIDERATIONS

PREGNANCY

Use ultrasound first; physiologic hydronephrosis can complicate interpretation. Avoid NSAIDs, use pregnancy-safe analgesia, and involve obstetrics/urology when infection, obstruction, persistent symptoms, or uncertain imaging occurs.
